knowledge_points.label: Three inference metrics: TTFT, latency, throughput
knowledge_points.statement: Inference speed is three different numbers: time-to-first-token (how long before any output, set by prefill), latency in seconds per token for one query, and throughput in tokens per second across many queries; interactive use cares about the first two, batch processing about the third.

anchors.quote: Time-to-first-token (TTFT): how long user waits before any generation happens (for interactive applications) ... Latency (seconds/token): how fast tokens appear for *one* query (for interactive applications) ... Throughput (tokens/second): how fast tokens appear for *many* queries (for batch processing)

Training (supervised): you see all tokens, can parallelize over sequence (matmul in Transformer) ... Inference: you have to generate sequentially, can't parallelize over generation, so harder to fully utilize compute
training is one-time cost, inference is repeated many times
time-to-first-token (TTFT) is essentially a function of prefill time

training is a one-time cost. ... But inference is a repeated cost. ... So OpenAI is estimated to produce 8.6 trillion tokens a day. ... So in less than four days, the number of tokens that OpenAI has to produce, and therefore the compute is at least DeepSeek-V4.
So most of the tokens that the agent produces is actually not for reading. ... But for an agent, there's no limit to how much a value you can get out of squeezing more out of inference.
as soon as tokens come in, it doesn't maybe have to be that fast, because if you're going to read it anyway, you can't read that fast.
So latency or one latency and throughput are clearly very related. ... But as we'll see later, there's actually a trade off here.

when you're doing training, you see all the tokens at once ... In inference, you can't do that. ... this is the fundamental problem of why inference is a very different workload than training, because you can't parallelize across the sequence dimension.

provenance.filtering_note: The landscape section (L63-L88) lists where inference shows up (chatbots, evaluation, RL), the '~8.6T tokens per day' and '32T tokens' figures (L70-L71, cited to an article and the DeepSeek-V4 report), providers and four open-source stacks (vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, llama.cpp, L83-L86). None of that is testable mechanism; only the three metrics and the sequential-generation observation are kept. The professor defines latency as seconds/token, not time per request. Spoken evidence (1:41-2:26): the 'one-time vs repeated' line (L69) gets its arithmetic aloud: at 8.6T tokens a day against DeepSeek-V4's 32T training tokens, inference matches the training token count 'in less than four days' (32 / 8.6 = 3.7). Spoken evidence (3:20-3:51, 5:40-6:00): why throughput matters more now: an agent's tokens are mostly 'not for reading', so there is no reading-speed ceiling, whereas a chatbot user mostly feels TTFT and the stream 'doesn't maybe have to be that fast' once it starts. Spoken evidence (6:28-6:46): latency and throughput usually improve together, with a trade-off (batch size) promised for later. The landscape (vLLM 'kind of a go-to', SGLang for agentic workloads, TensorRT 'more narrow', llama.cpp for CPU, 4:20-4:50) is narrated and still not a KP.

misconceptions.belief: A serving system that is 'fast' is fast on one number; improving throughput improves latency too.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The lecture separates per-query latency from aggregate throughput (L92-L93) precisely because the main lever, batch size, moves them in opposite directions (L360-L361).

misconceptions.belief: Time-to-first-token is just the latency of the first decode step.
misconceptions.why_wrong: TTFT is dominated by prefill, which processes the whole prompt before the first token can be emitted (L366); it scales with prompt length, not with the per-token decode cost.

predict.q: A chatbot provider doubles the batch size during generation and nothing else. Which of the three metrics gets worse for an individual user?
predict.why: Each decode step now reads a larger KV cache, so every token takes longer for everyone (L356); throughput improves because the parameter read is amortized over more tokens (L357). TTFT is a prefill quantity (L366).
predict.targets_misconception: A serving system that is 'fast' is fast on one number; improving throughput improves latency too.

transfer.q: You run an overnight job that scores 2 million short documents with a model, and separately a code-completion popup that must feel instant. Name the one metric each workload should optimize, with the one-phrase reason from the lecture.
transfer.answer: Overnight job: throughput (tokens/second across many queries, batch processing). Code completion: time-to-first-token (the user waits before any generation happens).
transfer.why: L91-L93 attach each metric to a use: TTFT and per-query latency to interactive applications, throughput to batch processing.

check.why: The wait before any output is time-to-first-token, set by prefill (L91); seconds per token governs the pace once speech starts, and throughput is the batch-processing metric (L93).
check.varies: a new interactive workload, where the requirement is on the start of output rather than on the overall job
check.invariant: TTFT, per-token latency and throughput are three different numbers, each tied to a different use

knowledge_points.label: MLP arithmetic intensity equals the batch (tokens) dimension
knowledge_points.statement: For X (B×D) @ W (D×F) in bf16 the intensity is 2BDF / (2BD + 2DF + 2BF), which tends to B when B is much smaller than D and F; so a matmul against shared weights is compute-bound only when the number of tokens exceeds the accelerator intensity (989e12 / 3.35e12 ≈ 295 on H100), and B = 1 (a matrix-vector product, intensity 1) is maximally memory-bound.

anchors.quote: assert flops == 2*B*D*F ... assert bytes_transferred == 2*B*D + 2*D*F + 2*B*F ... intensity = intensity.subs(D, c*B).subs(F, c*B).limit(c, oo).simplify() ... assert intensity == B
flops_per_second = 989e12 ... memory_bandwidth = 3.35e12 ... assert round(accelerator_intensity) == 295 ... Conclusion: compute-bound iff B > 295

Extreme case (B = 1, corresponding to matrix-vector product): ... Arithmetic intensity: 1 ... Memory-bound (read D x F matrix, perform only 2 D F FLOPs) ... This is basically what happens with inference...
assert flops == 6*B*T*D*F ... assert bytes_transferred == 4*B*T*D + 4*B*T*F + 6*D*F ... assert intensity == B*T

Prefill: easy to make compute-bound (good) by making `B*T` large enough (large batches, long sequences) ... Generating one token at a time (T = 1) ... B is number of concurrent requests, unpredictable for interactive applications
It's kind of a quadratic-like term, and matmuls are qubit. ... And remember, this is going to be important because that's how you're going to get high arithmetic intensity.
remember when we did arithmetic intensity for matmul, it was something like N/3. ... And this is the kind of analog, where instead of just having square matrices, we have non-square matrices.

You're reading this DF matrix, but B is only one. ... And this is basically the workload that you'll see in inference. ... You don't get these full matrices, you get these very thin matrices or tensors.
And it also makes sense because the batch dimension and the sequence length dimension are-- everything is independent. ... And for the MLP, they don't interact.

your arithmetic intensity is going to be B, but B in generation is the number of concurrent requests. ... So it's a bit unpredictable. ... So that's something we're going to address when we talk about continuous batching.

provenance.filtering_note: The limit is taken by substituting D = cB, F = cB and sending c to infinity (L143, L210), i.e. it assumes B (or B*T) is much smaller than D and F; for realistic decode batches that holds. The gated MLP accounting (L187-L202) counts three weight matrices (Wup, Wgate, Wdown) and the writes of U and G, giving 6BTDF FLOPs and 4BTD + 4BTF + 6DF bytes; the professor states the limit B*T without showing the intermediate simplified expression (@inspect at L208 is a sympy expression). The H100 constants (989e12 FLOP/s dense bf16, 3.35e12 B/s) are the same ones lecture 2 used; they are spec-sheet numbers, not measurements. Spoken evidence (16:51-17:04): the limit B is presented as the non-square analogue of lecture 2's n/3 for square matmuls (lecture_02:arithmetic-intensity). Spoken evidence (27:47-28:01): why the gated MLP's intensity is B·T: batch and sequence positions 'don't interact' in an MLP, so together they act as one token dimension. Spoken evidence (28:33-28:59): at generation T = 1, so the intensity is B, and B is 'the number of concurrent requests', which a chatbot server does not choose ('a bit unpredictable'); this is the motive given for continuous batching. bf16 is said to be 'the case for inference' (15:08). The gated-MLP accounting is not stepped through aloud (26:12).

external_prerequisites.note: L139 says 'Recall that arithmetic intensity is how much compute we do per byte transferred'; the definition and the 295 threshold were derived in lecture 2.
The 2BDF count is used without derivation (L132).
Every byte term carries a factor 2 'for bf16' (L128).

misconceptions.belief: A bigger model (larger D, F) has higher arithmetic intensity, so large models are compute-bound at decode.
misconceptions.why_wrong: In the limit the D and F factors cancel: intensity → B (L143-L144). Making the weight matrix larger increases FLOPs and bytes in the same proportion; only the number of tokens sharing the weight read changes the ratio.

misconceptions.belief: Decode is memory-bound because the GPU has too little memory.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Memory-bound here means bandwidth-bound: at B = 1 the whole D×F matrix is read from HBM to do only 2DF FLOPs (L158), so the time is set by bytes moved, regardless of how much memory the GPU has.

predict.q: You swap Llama 2 13B's MLP (D = 5120, F = 13824) for one four times wider (F = 55296) and keep decoding with 32 concurrent requests. In the professor's limit, how does the MLP arithmetic intensity change (up / down / same)?
predict.why: Intensity → B*T = 32 × 1 after the limit (L210-L211); F cancels between FLOPs (6BTDF) and the dominant byte term (6DF).
predict.targets_misconception: A bigger model (larger D, F) has higher arithmetic intensity, so large models are compute-bound at decode.

transfer.q: Decode on an H100 (989e12 FLOP/s, 3.35e12 B/s) with 64 concurrent requests, one token each. What is the MLP arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte) in the professor's limit?
transfer.why: Intensity = B*T = 64 × 1 (L211); the accelerator's intensity is 989e12 / 3.35e12 ≈ 295 (L149-L150), so this is about 4.6x short of compute-bound.

retrieval.q: What does the MLP arithmetic intensity simplify to when B*T is much smaller than D and F?
retrieval.answer: B*T (the number of tokens processed together).

retrieval.q: What is the H100 accelerator intensity the professor computes, and from which two numbers?
retrieval.answer: About 295, from 989e12 FLOP/s divided by 3.35e12 bytes/s.

retrieval.q: Why is the B = 1 case called a matrix-vector product, and what is its intensity?
retrieval.answer: X is a single row, so X @ W is one vector times a matrix; the whole D×F matrix is read for only 2DF FLOPs, intensity 1.

retrieval.q: What are the two reasons generation is hard to make compute-bound?
retrieval.answer: One token at a time (T = 1), and B is the number of concurrent requests, which is unpredictable for interactive applications.

In generation (T = 1) the MLP bar sits at about B and does not move when F is widened; it crosses the H100's 295 line only once B·T exceeds about 300 tokens.

knowledge_points.label: KV cache turns O(T^3) naive generation into prefill + sequential decode
knowledge_points.statement: Re-running the Transformer on the whole history for each new token costs O(T^3) FLOPs for T tokens; caching every layer's key and value vectors in HBM (one H-vector per sequence, token, layer and KV head) shares that work, splitting inference into a parallel prefill of the prompt and a sequential generation of one token per step.

anchors.quote: Naive inference: to generate each token, feed history into Transformer ... Complexity: generating T tokens requires O(T^3) FLOPs (one feedforward pass is O(T^2))

Observation: a lot of the work can be shared across prefixes ... Solution: store **KV cache** in HBM ... KV cache: for every sequence (B), token (S), layer (L), head (K), store an H-dimensional vector
Two stages of inference: ... **Prefill**: given a prompt, encode into vectors (parallelizable like in training) ... **Generation**: generate new response tokens (sequential)

anchors.ref: scaling-book inference chapter (naive-inference and cached-inference figures)

anchors.quote: each time you generate one token, you actually take order T squared time where T is the number of tokens that you've generated so far. ... So generate T tokens is actually T cubed because the attention is already T squared, and you have to do that once for every token.
the first obvious thing is to store a KV cache in HPM, so that, between successive token generations, you can just reuse the KV cache.

You encode the prompt into these vectors. ... And this is parallelizable just like in training because you see the entire prompt. ... But at least you don't have to pay for generating the KV cache of the tokens that you already looked at.
So k should be the number of groups, and g should be the number of the heads per one of those groups. ... I'll fix that later.

provenance.filtering_note: The two figures at L165 and L171 are the scaling book's; the professor does not derive the O(T^3) (it is sum over t of O(t^2) per pass). 'Head (K)' at L172 already uses the GQA letter for KV heads, defined in the notation review (L114: N = K G). The notation review (L100-L115) also fixes F = 4D, D = NH and S = T during training; those conventions are not separate KPs. The KV cache stores key and value, so the 'H-dimensional vector' at L172 is really two of them (L297 counts '2 for key + value'). Correction (21:28-21:45): the note above says the professor does not derive the O(T^3); he gives the one-line argument aloud: each step costs O(T^2) because 'the attention is already T squared', and 'you have to do that once for every token'. Spoken evidence (22:27-22:41): the reason prefix work can be shared is causality; that became the spoken KP kv-cache-needs-causality. Notation (19:03-20:23, Q&A): a student points out that the scaling-book diagram swaps K and G; he agrees ('k should be the number of groups, and g should be the number of the heads per one of those groups ... I'll fix that later'), which matches L114 (N = K G). The transformer-block review is kept short because students implemented it in Assignment 1 (13:05).

external_prerequisites.note: The attention accounting at L219 is 'focusing on the matrix multiplications with FlashAttention', i.e. it assumes the S×T score matrix never hits HBM.

misconceptions.belief: The KV cache stores past tokens' hidden states so the model can skip recomputing them entirely.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It stores the per-layer key and value projections, the only things past positions contribute to a new token's attention (L172, L297); the new token still runs through every layer's MLP and attention.

misconceptions.belief: Prefill and generation are the same computation at different sizes.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Prefill processes S prompt tokens in parallel like training and is compute-bound; generation processes one token per step and is memory-bound (L175-L176, L256). The lecture's techniques target generation.

predict.q: With a KV cache in place, you generate 2000 tokens instead of 1000 from the same prompt. Ignoring the prompt, by roughly what factor does total attention FLOPs for generation grow?
predict.why: Each decode step attends over all previous tokens, so step t costs O(t) and the sum over T steps is O(T^2); doubling T quadruples it. Without the cache it would be O(T^3), an 8x jump (L167).
predict.targets_misconception: The KV cache stores past tokens' hidden states so the model can skip recomputing them entirely.

transfer.q: A request has a 3000-token prompt and asks for a 50-token answer. Which stage dominates its time-to-first-token, and which stage dominates the user-visible seconds-per-token afterwards? Name the stage and the bound (compute- or memory-) for each.
transfer.answer: TTFT: prefill of the 3000 tokens, compute-bound. Seconds/token afterwards: generation, one token per step, memory-bound.
transfer.why: Prefill encodes the prompt in parallel (L175) and sets TTFT (L366); generation is sequential (L176) and memory-bound (L256).

check.q: A request has a 20-token prompt and asks for a 4,000-token story. Which stage dominates its total wall-clock time, and what bounds that stage?
check.why: Prefill of 20 tokens is one short parallel pass; the 4,000 tokens are produced one per step (L176), and each step re-reads the weights and KV cache for little arithmetic, so it is memory-bound (L256).
check.varies: prompt and output lengths are inverted (short prompt, long output) and total time is asked instead of TTFT
check.invariant: prefill processes the prompt in parallel and is compute-bound; generation is sequential and memory-bound
distractor_from: 'generation, compute-bound' <- misconception: 'Prefill and generation are the same computation at different sizes.'
'prefill, compute-bound' <- plausible: carries over the TTFT answer, where prefill dominates
check.targets_misconception: Prefill and generation are the same computation at different sizes.

retrieval.q: What is the FLOP complexity of generating T tokens with naive (no cache) inference, and why?
retrieval.answer: O(T^3): each of the T passes over the history costs O(T^2).

retrieval.q: List the four index dimensions over which the KV cache stores an H-dimensional vector.
retrieval.answer: Sequence (B), token (S), layer (L), KV head (K).

retrieval.q: With a KV cache in place, what does each forward pass process in prefill, and what in generation?
retrieval.answer: Prefill: all prompt tokens at once, in parallel like training. Generation: one new token per sequence per step, sequentially.

knowledge_points.label: The KV cache is exact only because attention is causal
knowledge_points.statement: A KV cache can be reused only because the Transformer is causal: each token's keys and values depend only on itself and earlier tokens, so appending a token leaves every cached K and V exactly unchanged; in a bidirectional model every earlier token attends to the new one, so its keys and values in every layer above the first change and nothing above layer 1 could be reused.

anchors.quote: A lot of the work can actually be shared across prefixes. ... you're actually computing a lot of the same key values for never going to give.

So these tokens, they shouldn't change, OK? ... And this is because it's a causal transformer. ... If it was bidirectional, then if you attach a token, then everything changes. ... But if it's causal, then the activations here don't change based on any tokens you append.

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only (22:24-22:41). The code states the observation ('a lot of the work can be shared across prefixes', L169) and the fix (store the KV cache, L170), but never says why the shared work stays valid; aloud: 'this is because it's a causal transformer. If it was bidirectional, then if you attach a token, then everything changes.' 'Everything changes' is slightly loose: in a bidirectional model the first layer's K and V are projections of each token's own embedding and do not change; every deeper layer's do, because their inputs attended to the new token. The statement and the check say so (author refinement). The prefix-LM transfer is the author's changed case. Placed after prefill-vs-decode, inside whose stretch it is said.

prerequisites.note: The cache whose validity is being explained.

misconceptions.belief: The KV cache is a generic engineering trick that works for any Transformer, including bidirectional ones.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It relies on causal masking. In a bidirectional model each earlier token attends to the newly appended token, so its hidden states, and hence its K and V in every layer above the first, change at every step (22:27-22:41).

misconceptions.belief: Reusing cached keys and values is an approximation: the old tokens' values change a little when a token is appended, but not enough to matter.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Under causal masking they do not change at all: a token cannot attend to later tokens, so its K and V are exactly the same however many tokens follow. The cache is exact.

predict.q: A bidirectional (BERT-style) model is used to generate text: after each new token is appended, the whole sequence is rerun with full attention in every layer. Can the earlier tokens' keys and values from the previous step be reused?
choices: No: above layer 1, every earlier token's K and V change
Yes: the earlier tokens are unchanged, so their K and V are
Only for tokens outside a recent window of the sequence
Partly: only the last layer's K and V need recomputing
predict.answer: No: above layer 1, every earlier token's K and V change
predict.why: With full attention every earlier token attends to the new one, so from layer 2 up their inputs, and hence their K and V, change. Only a causal model keeps them fixed: 'If it was bidirectional, then if you attach a token, then everything changes' (22:30).
predict.targets_misconception: The KV cache is a generic engineering trick that works for any Transformer, including bidirectional ones.
predict.distractor_from: 'Yes: tokens unchanged' <- misconception: the cache works for any Transformer (the tokens are the same, their contexts are not); 'recent window' <- confuses this with sliding-window attention; 'only the last layer' <- underestimates propagation: every layer from 2 up sees changed inputs

transfer.q: A prefix-LM attends bidirectionally within the prompt, while generated tokens attend causally to the prompt and to earlier generated tokens; prompt tokens never attend to generated ones. During generation, which keys and values can be cached and reused, and what change to the input would force recomputing the prompt's cache?
transfer.answer: All of them: prompt tokens never see generated tokens, so their K and V are fixed after prefill, and each generated token's K and V depend only on earlier tokens. Adding text inside the bidirectional prompt block (for example a new user turn treated as prompt) would change every prompt token's K and V above layer 1 and force recomputing that cache.
transfer.why: The cache is valid exactly where a token's attention cannot reach later tokens. In a prefix-LM that holds for the prompt with respect to generated tokens, but not for new text added inside the prompt.
transfer.varies: the attention mask: bidirectional inside the prompt, causal outside it
transfer.invariant: a cached K or V is reusable only if that token cannot attend to anything appended later

check.q: A 4-layer bidirectional encoder (every token attends to every token in every layer) has processed 100 tokens. You append one token and rerun. Layer 1's keys and values are projections of each token's own embedding. Counting one (token, layer) pair for each token's K and V in each layer, how many pairs must be computed in this step, including the new token's? Type only the number.
check.why: The new token needs K and V in all 4 layers (4). The 100 old tokens keep their layer-1 K and V, but in layers 2-4 their inputs attended to the new token, so 100 × 3 = 300 must be recomputed: 304 in total. A causal model with a cache computes only the new token's 4.
check.targets_misconception: The KV cache is a generic engineering trick that works for any Transformer, including bidirectional ones.
check.varies: surface: count the recomputation instead of answering yes or no
check.invariant: a token's K and V must be recomputed whenever anything it attends to (directly or through lower layers) changes

retrieval.q: Why does appending a token leave the cached keys and values unchanged in a decoder-only Transformer?
retrieval.answer: Causal masking: a token's keys and values depend only on itself and earlier tokens, so later tokens cannot change them.

retrieval.q: What would break the KV cache in a bidirectional model?
retrieval.answer: Every earlier token attends to the new token, so its hidden states, and hence its K and V in every layer above the first, change at each step.

knowledge_points.label: Attention intensity ST/(S+T): batching does not help at decode
knowledge_points.statement: Attention over S cached tokens for T new tokens does 4BSTD FLOPs against 4BSD + 4BTD bytes, intensity ST/(S+T) with no B: prefill (T = S) gives S/2, generation (T = 1) gives S/(S+1) < 1, and because every sequence reads its own KV cache, adding concurrent requests cannot raise it.

anchors.quote: assert flops == 4*B*S*T*D ... assert bytes_transferred == 4*B*S*D + 4*B*T*D ... assert intensity == S*T / (S + T)

Unlike MLPs, no dependence on B, so batching doesn't help! ... In MLP layers, every sequence hits the same MLP weights (Wup, Wgate, Wdown don't depend on B) ... In attention layers, every sequence has its own KV cache vectors (Q, K, V all depend on B)

knowledge_points.label: Decode napkin math: latency = memory / bandwidth, throughput = B / latency
knowledge_points.statement: Because each decode step must read all parameters plus the whole KV cache, the best-case step latency is (2·params + B·kv_per_seq) / memory_bandwidth and throughput is B divided by that; for Llama 2 13B on an H100 (3.35e12 B/s) evaluating the formula gives 8.0 ms and 125 tokens/s at B = 1.

anchors.quote: *Latency* is determined by memory IO (read all parameters and KV cache for each step) ... latency = memory / memory_bandwidth ... *Throughput* is the inverse of latency, but we're generating B tokens in parallel ... throughput = B / latency

So we have shown that inference is memory-bound. ... Let us now compute the theoretical maximum latency and throughput of a single request. ... Assumption: can overlap compute and communication perfectly and ignore overhead. ... Instantiate latency and throughput for Llama 2 13B on an H100

knowledge_points.label: Batch size trades latency for throughput, with diminishing returns
knowledge_points.statement: Raising the decode batch size worsens every user's latency (more KV cache to read per step) but raises throughput (the parameter read is amortized over more tokens) with diminishing returns as the KV term dominates; so use small batches for prefill (TTFT) and large batches for generation, and launching M independent copies raises throughput M-fold without touching latency.

Use smaller batch sizes during prefill for faster TTFT ... Use larger batch sizes during generation to improve throughput

latency is a linear function in B. This is where the constant is the size of KV cache, and then this is the number of parameters. ... And then throughput is some proportional to B over B plus something.

fast actually has two meanings here, which actually, depending on which one you care about, is completely opposite. ... If you want to tune your batch size, that's going to really determine if you want latency or throughput.
your memory, you run out of memory because the memory, for storing this KV cache, is going to exceed your H100 memory. ... You'll never get to the asymptote because you'll hit the memory.

if you're an individual query, you have to wait for everyone to finish. ... you're waiting for a bus, and the latency is pretty high. ... Whereas, the throughput of a bus is pretty good because you can move everyone at once.
if you launch M copies of the model, the latency is the same, and the throughput increases by M.

misconceptions.belief: GQA speeds up decode because attention does fewer FLOPs.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Each of the N query heads still attends over the full cache; the saving is K·H instead of N·H key/value bytes per token per layer (L387), which matters because decode is bandwidth-bound (L388).

misconceptions.belief: MQA (K = 1) is strictly better than GQA for serving.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It gives the largest cache reduction but the lecture checks accuracy separately (L404-L405) and later notes MHA beats GQA in quality (L416); GQA is the middle point on that accuracy/size tradeoff (L381).

predict.q: Llama 2 13B keeps N = 40 query heads but moves from K = 40 to K = 8 KV heads. Ignoring the parameter-count change, by what factor does the KV cache per token shrink?
predict.why: Factor N/K = 40 / 8 (L387); per token the cache goes from 819,200 to 163,840 bytes (L297).
predict.targets_misconception: GQA speeds up decode because attention does fewer FLOPs.

transfer.q: A 70B-class model has L = 80, N = 64, H = 128 and uses GQA with K = 8, bf16. How many KV-cache bytes per token does it store?
transfer.why: Per token: K × H × L × 2 × 2 = 8 × 128 × 80 × 4 = 327,680 bytes (L297). MHA would set K = N = 64 (L379): 2,621,440 bytes, N/K = 8x more (L387).

retrieval.q: What value of K corresponds to MHA, and what value to MQA?
retrieval.answer: MHA: K = N. MQA: K = 1.

retrieval.q: By what factor does GQA reduce the KV cache, and why does that translate into speed?
retrieval.answer: N/K; because decode is memory-bound, fewer bytes means less time.

retrieval.q: What does cross-layer attention share, by analogy with what GQA shares?
retrieval.answer: KVs across layers, as GQA shares KVs across heads.

prompts.self_explain: Why does a K = 8 model need a separate accuracy check when its arithmetic is otherwise identical to the K = 40 model?

presentations.notice: Lowering K from 40 to 8 flattens the KV-cache growth line by 5x while the weight bar barely moves; the 80 GB crossing moves from about 66k to about 350k cached tokens.
listen for: cutting memory improves latency and throughput together; only batch size trades one for the other
Switching MHA to GQA shrinks the blue per-token bar by N/K (5× at K = 8) and multiplies the sequences that fit by about the same factor; the weight bar stays put.

knowledge_points.label: MLA caches a compressed latent c and up-projects K, V on demand
knowledge_points.statement: Multi-head latent attention stores per token a low-dimensional latent c = W_c h instead of the full K and V, recomputing K = W_K c and V = W_V c when needed; DeepSeek-V2 compresses N·H = 16384 to C = 512, adding 64 dimensions for RoPE (576 total) because the compression is not compatible with rotary embeddings.

anchors.quote: Normal attention: KV cache consists of K = W_K h, V = W_V h (N*H dimensions) ... MLA: store compressed vector c = W_c h (C dimensions), project up to K = W_K c, V = W_V c when needed

DeepSeek v2: reduce N*H = 16384 to C = 512 ... Wrinkle: MLA is not compatible with RoPE, so need to add additional 64 dimensions for RoPE, so 512 + 64 = 576 total dimensions ... Latency/throughput improvements follow similarly from the KV cache reduction as argued earlier
First, MHA is better than GQA (though more expensive) [Table 8] ... Second, MLA is even a bit better than MHA (and much cheaper) [Table 9]

anchors.ref: DeepSeek-V2 paper, Tables 8 and 9 (shown at L417, L419)

anchors.quote: So MLA says I'm going to actually project these activations down into C dimensions. ... So DeepSeek-V2 reduced it from 16,000 to 512, so this is quite aggressive compression here. ... So now, I can just store C. This is much smaller.
MLA is not compatible with rope, which operates directly on the keys and values. ... So what they do is add additional dimensions for handling the rope.
So the latency and throughput improvements follow by just simple math. ... The smaller the KV cache, the faster you go. ... It's almost kind of linear scaling up until at some point.

These ablations don't show that. ... My guess is that reducing the model dimension just makes things worse because you're indiscriminately just reducing everything. ... I think the trick in all of this kind of is to find places in the model where you can squeeze.

provenance.filtering_note: The accuracy tables (images/mla-accuracy.png, mla-accuracy2.png) are the paper's and are not restated; only the professor's two reading-off sentences are kept. He does not explain why RoPE is incompatible (the rotation depends on position and cannot be folded into W_c), nor that the up-projection W_K can be absorbed into the query projection so K is never materialized; both are in the paper. Per layer per token, MHA caches 2·N·H = 32768 values versus MLA's 576, about 57x fewer (author computation from L409-L412; the paper describes this as equivalent to GQA with 2.25 groups). Spoken evidence (53:36-53:52): the speed-up 'follow[s] by just simple math': the smaller the KV cache, the faster, 'almost kind of linear scaling up until at some point' (while decode stays memory-bound). Spoken evidence (55:02-55:27, Q&A): asked how MLA compares with shrinking the model dimension, he says the ablations do not show it and guesses that uniform shrinking is worse; 'the trick ... is to find places in the model where you can squeeze' (hedged, not part of this KP). Spoken slip (53:14): RoPE is said to operate 'directly on the keys and values'; RoPE rotates queries and keys, not values. Not imported. The note's 'does not explain why RoPE is incompatible' stands; '16,000' (52:50) is L412's 16384 rounded.

prerequisites.note: MLA is presented as the next step after GQA in reducing the cache, and compared against GQA and MHA (L416-L418).

external_prerequisites.note: MLA was introduced as an architecture choice in lecture 4; lecture 10 reuses it as a KV-cache reducer and adds the RoPE wrinkle and the accuracy tables.

misconceptions.belief: MLA is a form of GQA: it shares a few KV heads across queries.
misconceptions.why_wrong: MLA keeps all heads but stores a learned low-rank latent c of dimension C and regenerates per-head K and V from it (L410); the saving is C versus N·H, not K versus N.

misconceptions.belief: Because MLA stores less, it must lose accuracy relative to MHA.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The professor reads off Table 9 that MLA is 'even a bit better than MHA (and much cheaper)' (L418); the compression is learned, not a truncation.

predict.q: DeepSeek-V2 attention has N·H = 16384. Per layer per token, MHA caches both K and V. Compared with MLA's 576-dimensional cache, is MHA's cache about 28x, 57x, or 114x larger?
predict.why: MHA stores K and V, 2 × 16384 = 32768 values (L409); MLA stores one 576-dim vector (L412); 32768 / 576 ≈ 56.9. Choosing 28x forgets that both K and V are cached.
predict.targets_misconception: MLA is a form of GQA: it shares a few KV heads across queries.

transfer.q: A model with 60 layers uses MLA with C = 512 plus 64 RoPE dimensions, bf16 cache. How many KV-cache bytes per token?
transfer.why: Per token: (512 + 64) × 60 layers × 2 bytes = 69,120 (L412), one latent per layer replacing both K and V. A single 128k-token (131,072) context is then about 9.06 GB.

retrieval.q: What does MLA store in the cache, and what does it compute from it at attention time?
retrieval.answer: A compressed vector c = W_c h; K = W_K c and V = W_V c are projected up when needed.

retrieval.q: Why is the DeepSeek-V2 latent 576 and not 512 dimensions?
retrieval.answer: MLA is not compatible with RoPE, so 64 extra dimensions are added for RoPE.

retrieval.q: How does the professor rank MHA, GQA and MLA on accuracy from the two DeepSeek-V2 tables?
retrieval.answer: MHA better than GQA; MLA a bit better than MHA while much cheaper.

prompts.self_explain: Why can a learned projection W_c compress K and V together but not the position-dependent rotation RoPE applies to them?

presentations.notice: listen for: store a 512-dimensional latent per token and rebuild K and V from it when needed
With N = H = 128 the MLA bar (512 + 64 values per layer) is about 57× shorter than the MHA bar, which holds both K and V (2 × 16384 values).

knowledge_points.label: Local (sliding-window) attention caps the KV cache independent of length
knowledge_points.statement: If each layer attends only to a local window, the KV cache per sequence is bounded by the window rather than growing with sequence length, and information still propagates because the effective context grows linearly with depth; since pure local attention hurts accuracy, models interleave local layers with global ones.

anchors.quote: Idea: just look at the local context, which is most relevant for modeling ... Effective context scales linearly with the number of layers ... KV cache is independent of sequence length! ... Problem: this can still hurt accuracy ... Solution: interleave local attention with global attention (hybrid layers)

Goal: reduce the KV cache size (since inference is memory-bound) without hurting accuracy ... Lower-dimensional KV cache (GQA, MLA, CLA) ... Local attention (truncates the KV cache) on some of the layers ... Other ideas: linear attention / state-space-models (Mamba 2, GatedDeltaNet), diffusion models

DeepSeek v4 attention ... Supports 1M context length ... Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA): compresses every m tokens into 1 ... DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA): selects the top k ... Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA): compresses even more

For every token you generate, you just depend on the last K. ... So the KV cache is now independent of the sequence length. ... It's just the number of the batch times the other variables, which is great.
because of the number of layers, the effective context length is actually larger than the number of the stated context length because information can propagate farther in if you go down the layers.

the problem with this is that it actually still hurts accuracy. ... There's no free lunch here, or at least this was an expensive lunch. ... So the solution that people come up with is that they interleave local attention with global attention.

So compressed attention is going to basically compress every M tokens into one token. ... DeepSeek sparse attention, which basically selects a subset of those to keep. ... So a lightning fast way to figure out what tokens you need to keep.

provenance.filtering_note: Three papers are linked at L427 without saying which claim comes from which; the window figure is Longformer's. 'Effective context scales linearly with the number of layers' (L430) is asserted, not derived: with window W, after l layers a position can be influenced by tokens up to l·W back. The DeepSeek-V4 CSA/DSA/HCA bullets (L438-L440) are three names with one-phrase glosses and the figure deepseek-v4-attention.png; they are kept as anchors for the summary 'truncate or compress the cache' but are not separately testable. Linear attention / SSMs / diffusion (L446) are named only. Spoken evidence (57:51-58:05): the linear-in-depth reach (L430) gets its reason aloud, 'information can propagate farther in if you go down the layers', still without the l·W arithmetic. Spoken evidence (58:27-58:47): local attention 'still hurts accuracy ... There's no free lunch', hence the interleaving. Spoken evidence (1:02:56-1:03:32): the DeepSeek-V4 bullets are narrated from the figure: CSA compresses every m tokens into one, DSA selects a subset with a small indexer attention ('a lightning fast way to figure out what tokens you need to keep'), then more compression, cut short 'in the interest of time' (1:03:40). The window is called 'the last K tokens' (57:14), reusing K, which elsewhere in this lecture counts KV heads. Linear attention, Mamba and DeltaNet come up only in Q&A (59:13-1:02:14), as more expressive than a sliding window but lossy on needle-in-a-haystack recall (lecture_04 thread).

prerequisites.note: The S factor in S·(K·H)·L·2·2 is what the window replaces.

external_prerequisites.note: 'Interleave local attention with global attention (hybrid layers)' (L433) is the same hybrid-layer pattern lecture 4 taught for linear/SSM layers.
DSA 'selects the top k' (L439) is the sparse-attention indexer from lecture 4.
'linear attention / state-space-models (Mamba 2, GatedDeltaNet)' (L446) are named only here; lecture 4 has the mechanism.

misconceptions.belief: With a window of W tokens, the model can only ever use the last W tokens of context.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Information propagates one window per layer, so the receptive field after L layers is about L·W tokens (L430); what is bounded is the cache per layer, not the model's reach.

misconceptions.belief: Sliding-window attention is a free KV-cache reduction with no quality cost.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The lecture flags that it 'can still hurt accuracy' (L432) and that production models interleave global layers (L433); the summary says 'on some of the layers' (L445).

predict.q: A 32-layer model attends with a 4096-token sliding window in every layer. A request has 100,000 tokens of context. How many tokens' worth of K and V does each layer hold in the cache?
predict.why: Local attention truncates the cache to the window regardless of sequence length (L431, L445); the 100k context only enters through the window-per-layer propagation (L430).
predict.targets_misconception: With a window of W tokens, the model can only ever use the last W tokens of context.

transfer.q: Same 32-layer model, window 4096. A system interleaves one global-attention layer after every three local layers (8 global, 24 local). At a 32k-token context in bf16 with K = 8, H = 128, what is the KV cache per sequence compared with the all-global model, as a decimal fraction (e.g. 0.5)?
transfer.why: Each layer's cache is tokens × K·H·2·2 (L297); local layers hold the window (L431), global layers hold the full context (L433). The per-token constant cancels in the ratio.

retrieval.q: How does the effective context of a sliding-window model grow?
retrieval.answer: Linearly with the number of layers.

retrieval.q: What is the lecture's remedy for the accuracy loss of local attention?
retrieval.answer: Interleave local attention with global attention (hybrid layers).

retrieval.q: Name the two families of KV-cache reduction in the lecture's section summary and one example of each.
retrieval.answer: Lower-dimensional cache (GQA, MLA, CLA); local attention truncating the cache on some layers.

prompts.self_explain: Why would a local layer and a global layer stacked together recover much of what pure local attention loses?

presentations.notice: listen for: local attention costs accuracy, so models interleave it with global layers
With a window set, the green local layers stop at W tokens however long S gets, while the blue global layers keep growing with S; the per-sequence total is their mix.

knowledge_points.label: Quantization: scale and zero point, dtype bytes, QAT vs PTQ
knowledge_points.statement: Quantization maps x to round(x / scale) + zero_point and back to (q − zero_point) · scale, trading precision for bytes (bf16 2 B, fp8/int8 1 B, int4 0.5 B), which speeds memory-bound decode; it is either trained in (QAT, simulate quantize-dequantize in the forward pass) or applied after training (PTQ, calibrate scale and zero point on sample data; GPTQ uses Hessian information to update the not-yet-quantized weights to compensate for quantization error; AWQ uses activation statistics to protect the salient weight channels).

anchors.quote: Key idea: reduce the precision of numbers ... Less memory means higher latency/throughput (since inference is memory-bound).

x = 5.2342  # @inspect x ... scale = 0.1 ... zero_point = 4 ... x_quant = round(x / scale) + zero_point  # Quantize  @inspect x_quant ... x_approx = (x_quant - zero_point) * scale  # Dequantize @inspect x_approx

fp32 (4 bytes): needed for parameters and optimizer states during training ... bf16 (2 bytes): default for inference ... fp8 (1 byte) [-240, 240] for e4m3 on H100s: can train if you dare ... int8 (1 byte) [-128, 127]: less accurate but cheaper than fp8, but for inference only ... int4 (0.5 bytes) [-8, 7]: cheaper, even less accurate

Quantization-aware training (QAT) ... During training, quantize-and-dequantize during the forward pass to simulate quantization errors ... Post-training quantization (PTQ): ... Run on sample data to determine scale and zero point for each layer or tensor ... GPTQ: use Hessian information to update non-quantized weights to account for quantization error

Observation: some activation channels are large ... Weights that hit those matter more ... Idea: select which weights (0.1-1%) to keep in high precision based on activations ... fp16 → int3 produces 4x lower memory, 3.2x speedup
you train a model with quantization in mind. ... during the feedforward pass during training, you quantize and dequantize ... But the con is that it requires expensive large-scale training.

for every layer or tensor, you basically determine the scale and the 0 point for each, let's say, tensor. ... This generally doesn't work as well. ... GPTQ, which uses some Hessian information to quantize layer by layer. ... errors which get propagated into the non-quantized weights.
And some of these activation channels are large. ... you basically allocate like, let's say, fp16 for this channel. ... You keep everything else as in three.
Less memory means higher latency and throughput.

provenance.filtering_note: The worked example is plain Python: 5.2342 / 0.1 = 52.342, round → 52, + 4 → x_quant = 56; x_approx = (56 − 4) × 0.1 = 5.2 (so the error is 0.0342, half a step at most). The dtype image (L461) is Baseten's and the fp8 training paper and fp8-vs-int8 paper are linked for the ranges (L464-L466); the code's '[-240, 240] for e4m3 on H100s' (L464) is a slip: the H100's E4M3 (OCP FP8) reaches ±448, as lecture 2 says; ±240 is the maximum of the e4m3 'fnuz' variant used on some other accelerators (corrected 2026-10-02). 'fp16 → int3 produces 4x lower memory, 3.2x speedup' (L486) is AWQ's own reported number, read by the professor; it is quoted here as the paper's claim, not asserted. The lecture says 'higher latency/throughput' at L451 where it means lower latency / higher throughput. Which layers or tensors share one scale (per-tensor vs per-channel vs per-group) is not discussed. Correction (1:05:59-1:06:15): the note above says per-tensor vs per-channel scaling 'is not discussed'. Partly it is: one scale and zero point per layer or tensor is presented as the naive PTQ, which 'generally doesn't work as well'; per-channel and per-group are still not mentioned. Spoken evidence (1:06:18-1:06:33): GPTQ is described as L475 describes it: Hessian information, layer by layer, with the quantization error 'propagated into the non-quantized weights'. That is error compensation, not choosing weights to protect, so the statement's 'GPTQ and AWQ decide which weights to protect' fits AWQ only (flagged for review; the statement is unchanged because no written material was corrected). Spoken evidence (1:07:16-1:07:39): AWQ walked through on the figure: a few large-activation channels stay fp16, everything else int3. Spoken slip (1:04:48): 'Less memory means higher latency and throughput', repeating L451's wording where lower latency is meant. Not imported.

prerequisites.note: 'Less memory means higher latency/throughput (since inference is memory-bound)' (L451) is the bytes / bandwidth model.

external_prerequisites.note: fp32 / bf16 / fp8 byte widths were introduced there; int8 and int4 are new here.

misconceptions.belief: Quantizing weights to int8 halves decode latency because int8 arithmetic is twice as fast.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The lecture's argument is about bytes, not arithmetic (L451): decode is memory-bound, so halving the weight bytes halves the parameter-read term in latency = memory / bandwidth; the KV cache term is unchanged unless it is quantized too.

misconceptions.belief: Post-training quantization needs no data.
misconceptions.why_wrong: PTQ runs on sample data to determine the scale and zero point per layer or tensor (L477), and AWQ uses activation statistics to pick which weights to protect (L482-L485).

predict.q: Using the lecture's scheme with scale = 0.1 and zero_point = 4, quantize x = −2.37 (giving the integer x_quant) and dequantize it. What is x_approx, the dequantized value?
predict.why: x_quant: round(−2.37 / 0.1) = round(−23.7) = −24; −24 + 4 = −20 (L458). Dequantize: (−20 − 4) × 0.1 = −2.4 (L459). The error 0.03 is under half a step.

transfer.q: Llama 2 13B (13.0e9 parameters) is served at B = 1, short context, on an H100 (3.35e12 B/s). Under the napkin model, what is the per-token latency bound in milliseconds with int4 weights (KV cache ignored)?
transfer.why: Bytes per parameter 0.5 for int4 vs 2 for bf16 (L463, L466); latency = bytes / bandwidth (L303): 0.5 × 13.0e9 / 3.35e12 ≈ 1.9 ms versus 2 × 13.0e9 / 3.35e12 ≈ 7.8 ms in bf16, 4x lower. The 4x is the memory ratio; the real speedup is smaller because the KV cache and overheads are not quantized away.

retrieval.q: Write the quantize and dequantize formulas the lecture uses.
retrieval.answer: x_quant = round(x / scale) + zero_point; x_approx = (x_quant − zero_point) × scale.

retrieval.q: How many bytes per number are fp32, bf16, fp8/int8 and int4?
What does QAT do during the forward pass, and what is its stated con?
retrieval.answer: Quantize-and-dequantize to simulate quantization error; it requires expensive large-scale training.

retrieval.q: On what basis does AWQ choose the 0.1-1% of weights to keep in high precision?
retrieval.answer: Activations: weights that multiply large activation channels matter more.

prompts.self_explain: Why does the professor repeat 'since inference is memory-bound' when introducing quantization, and what would quantization buy during compute-bound prefill?

steps.why: scale is the real-valued size of one integer step, so this expresses x in steps.

steps.do: L458: round, then add the zero point.
steps.why: Rounding is where the precision is lost; the zero point sets which integer stands for 0.0, so the stored integers can sit in the type's range.

steps.do: L459: dequantize by subtracting the zero point and multiplying by the scale.
steps.why: These undo the shift and the division exactly; only the rounding cannot be undone.
Round-to-nearest is off by at most scale/2, so a smaller scale buys precision at the cost of range.

presentations.notice: listen for: naive per-tensor PTQ versus GPTQ pushing each error into the weights not yet quantized
Switching bf16 to int4 weights at B = 1 cuts the bytes per step, and so the latency, by 4×; at large B the KV read dominates and the same switch helps little.

knowledge_points.label: Pruning: remove layers/heads/dims, then distill from the original
knowledge_points.statement: Pruning makes a cheaper model by scoring the importance of layers, heads and hidden dimensions on a small calibration set, removing the unimportant ones, and then repairing the smaller model by distilling the original into it; this is the lecture's 'distillation recipe' for faster architectures as opposed to training a faster model from scratch.

anchors.quote: Key idea: just rip out parts of an expensive model to make it cheaper ... and then fix it up.
Identify important {layer, head, hidden dimension} on a small calibration dataset (1024 samples) ... Remove unimportant layers to get a smaller model ... Distill the original model into pruned model

From scratch recipe: ... Define faster model architecture ... Train faster model ... Distillation recipe: ... Initialize weights using original model (which has a different architecture) ... Repair faster model (distillation)

anchors.ref: NVIDIA pruning + distillation paper (loop and results figures shown at L495, L502)

anchors.quote: So here you just take a large model, and you rip out pieces of it, and you fix it up. ... It's a very crude way, but it turns out to work.

you first have to estimate the importance of the different parts of the model and choose the most important parts. ... And then you basically remove different hidden units and different even layers. ... You train it some more on the data or the tasks that you care about to heal it.

you have a calibration set, and you pass the inputs through the model. ... And you're basically looking at the magnitude of the activations. ... especially if they're dead units, will be kind of close to 0. ... And the ones that are large, you want to keep.
So they were able to take a 15B model and reduce it to an 8B model. ... And it doesn't really hurt accuracy by too much.

provenance.filtering_note: The section is a stub: it ends with '# TODO' at L504 and all results are in images/pruning-kd.png, which is the paper's and is not restated. The professor's step 2 says 'Remove unimportant layers' although step 1 scores layers, heads and hidden dimensions; the paper prunes along all three axes. How importance is scored (activation statistics on the calibration set) and what distillation loss is used are not stated. The 'From scratch' vs 'Distillation' recipes (L34-L41) sit in main() as the bridge between the KV-cache section and the lossy shortcuts; they are anchored here because pruning is their worked instance. Correction (1:10:05-1:10:28, Q&A): the note above says how importance is scored 'is not stated'. Aloud: pass a calibration set through the model and look at 'the magnitude of the activations'; near-zero ('dead') units go, large ones stay. In follow-ups he adds that this rests on the empirical fact that some channels are much larger than others (1:10:43-1:11:03), and that a constant high-mean, low-variance unit might be folded into a bias rather than removed (1:11:24-1:11:43, hedged). Spoken evidence (1:08:14): what is removed is 'different hidden units and different even layers', matching the paper's several axes rather than L497's 'layers'. The repair is described as training 'some more ... to heal it' and, in the summary, as distillation (1:09:39). The 15B to 8B result is the paper's, read aloud (1:08:55), and is not restated. 'a training way to reduce the KV cache' (1:08:37) is loose: pruning shrinks the parameters, and the KV cache only where layers or KV heads are removed.

misconceptions.belief: Pruning a model is a post-processing step that needs no further training.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The algorithm's third step distills the original model into the pruned one to repair it (L499, L41); the lecture's phrase is 'rip out parts ... and then fix it up' (L491-L492).

misconceptions.belief: Distillation requires the student to have the same architecture as the teacher.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The distillation recipe explicitly initializes a model 'which has a different architecture' from the original's weights and then repairs it (L39-L41).

predict.q: You prune 25% of a model's layers using importance scores from 1024 calibration samples and immediately evaluate it. Relative to the original and to the final distilled model, where does its accuracy sit?
choices: below the original, recovered by distillation
below the original, and distillation cannot help
predict.answer: below the original, recovered by distillation
predict.why: Removing parts damages the model; the recipe's third step, distilling the original into the pruned model, is what repairs it (L497-L499).
predict.targets_misconception: Pruning a model is a post-processing step that needs no further training.

transfer.q: A team wants a 4B model from an existing 8B model and has a budget far below pretraining a 4B model. Lay out the three steps the lecture's recipe prescribes and say what plays the role of the teacher.
transfer.answer: 1. Score layers, heads and hidden dimensions on a small calibration set; 2. remove the unimportant ones to reach a 4B architecture, initializing from the 8B weights; 3. distill the 8B model (teacher) into the pruned 4B model (student).
transfer.why: L497-L499 and the distillation recipe at L38-L41: initialize from the original, then repair by distillation.

check.q: A 70B model has just been pruned to 40B by removing low-importance layers and heads scored on a small calibration set, and its accuracy has dropped. Which step does the lecture's recipe run next?
choices: Distill the 40B model into the 70B model
Deploy the 40B model; pruning is done
Distill the 70B model into the 40B model
check.answer: Distill the 70B model into the 40B model
check.why: The recipe initializes the small model from the original's weights and repairs it by distillation with the original as teacher (L497-L499, L38-L41); pruning alone leaves the accuracy drop in place.
check.varies: model sizes and the question (the next step after pruning, rather than the whole recipe)
check.invariant: prune from the original, then repair by distilling the original (teacher) into the pruned model (student)
distractor_from: 'Deploy the 40B model; pruning is done' <- misconception: 'Pruning a model is a post-processing step that needs no further training.'
'Pretrain the 40B model from scratch' <- plausible: ignores that the recipe initializes from the original weights
'Distill the 40B model into the 70B model' <- plausible: swaps teacher and student
check.targets_misconception: Pruning a model is a post-processing step that needs no further training.

retrieval.q: Along which three structural axes does the pruning algorithm identify important components?
retrieval.answer: Layer, head, hidden dimension.

retrieval.q: How large is the calibration dataset in the lecture's pruning recipe?
retrieval.answer: 1024 samples.

retrieval.q: The lecture's from-scratch recipe defines a faster architecture and trains it. What does the distillation recipe do instead after defining the faster architecture?
retrieval.answer: It initializes the faster model's weights from the original model (despite the different architecture), then repairs the faster model by distillation from the original.

knowledge_points.label: Speculative sampling: cheap draft proposes, target verifies in parallel
knowledge_points.statement: Because verifying tokens is a parallel, compute-bound prefill while generating them is a sequential, memory-bound loop, a cheap draft model p proposes a few tokens (e.g. 4) and the target model q scores all of them in one pass, keeping the accepted prefix and always producing at least one token, so several tokens come out per expensive target step.

anchors.quote: Prefill: given a sequence, encode tokens in parallel (compute-bound) [note: also gives you probabilities] ... Generation: generate one token at a time (memory-bound) ... In other words, checking is faster than generation.
Use a cheaper **draft model** p to guess a few tokens (e.g., 4) ... Evaluate with target model q (process tokens in parallel), and accept if it looks good

This is modified rejection sampling with proposal p and target q ... Modification: always generate at least one candidate (rejection sampling will keep looping) ... Key property: guaranteed to be an **exact sample** from the target model!
Target model has 70B parameters, draft model has 8B parameters ... Target model has 8B parameters, draft model has 1B parameters ... Try to make draft model as close to target (distillation)
Medusa: draft model generates multiple tokens in parallel ... EAGLE: draft model takes high-level features from target model

anchors.ref: Chen et al. 2023 (algorithm figure shown at L519)

anchors.quote: So checking is faster than generation. ... If I give you a sequence, it's fast to tell me how good it is, much faster than it is to generate one at a time. ... So you can exploit this asymmetry

So things are kind of chosen to be balanced. ... The draft model is just smaller and cheaper. ... And so even though it's memory-bound, and it has to generate one at a time, is not too bad. ... Whereas, the target model is big and expensive

ideally, you want the model draft model to be as close to the target, which means that you want to distill it ... If you're not happy with it, then it at least can be a draft model and you can use your main model to fix things up.

provenance.filtering_note: The algorithm itself is an image (images/speculative-sampling-algorithm.png) plus a linked video and blog; the results and stats figures (L534-L535) are the papers' wall-clock speedups and acceptance rates and are not restated. The professor does not state the expected tokens per target pass; the fixture notice uses 1 + (number accepted), which follows from 'always generate at least one candidate' (L521): on the first rejection a token is drawn from the residual, and if all k are accepted the target's extra position yields one more. He also does not say that the draft must run sequentially k times (its cost is small because it is small, L538-L539). Medusa and EAGLE are one line each (L543-L544). Correction (1:12:50-1:13:11): the note above says he 'does not say that the draft must run sequentially k times'. He does: the draft, 'even though it's memory-bound, and it has to generate one at a time, is not too bad' because it is small, while the big target processes the drafted tokens in parallel; the two costs are 'chosen to be balanced'. Spoken evidence (1:12:16-1:12:26): the asymmetry in one line, 'checking is faster than generation'. Spoken evidence (1:16:04-1:16:43): the draft should be distilled to be close to the target, so the lecture's KV-cache-reduction tricks double as ways to build drafts: a reduced model you are not happy serving 'at least can be a draft model'. Later methods (Medusa, EAGLE, L542-L544) are skipped aloud (1:16:43).

prerequisites.note: 'checking is faster than generation' (L511) restates prefill (parallel) versus generation (sequential).
Scoring k draft tokens in one pass raises T from 1 to k+1 at almost no extra time because the step was bandwidth-bound; this is the intensity = B*T argument.

misconceptions.belief: Speculative sampling saves time by running the big model less often on average while slightly changing its outputs.
misconceptions.why_wrong: The outputs are exact samples from the target distribution (L522); the saving comes from the target scoring k+1 positions in one memory-bound pass instead of k+1 passes (L515, L511).

misconceptions.belief: Verifying 4 draft tokens costs the target model about 4 times a normal decode step.
misconceptions.why_wrong: A decode step is memory-bound: its time is set by reading weights and cache, which happens once per pass regardless of whether 1 or 5 positions are scored (L509-L511, L303).

The pass costs about one ordinary decode step, since the target scored all positions in one parallel, memory-bound pass (L515, L511).

transfer.why: Tokens per target pass is 1 + accepted (always at least one, L521); plain decoding yields one token per pass. The draft's 4 sequential small-model steps eat into this in practice (L538).

knowledge_points.label: Why speculative sampling is exact: accept q/p, resample from max(q−p, 0)
knowledge_points.statement: A draft token x is accepted with probability min(1, q(x)/p(x)) and on rejection a token is drawn from the normalized residual max(q − p, 0); summing the two routes gives P[x] = q(x) exactly, as the two-token example shows: P[A] = p(A)·q(A)/p(A) = q(A) and P[B] = p(B) + p(A)(1 − q(A)/p(A)) = q(B).

anchors.quote: Proof by example: assume two vocabulary elements {A, B} ... Assume p(A) > q(A) [draft model oversamples A]. ... Therefore p(B) < q(B) [draft model undersamples B]. ... Residual probabilities max(q-p, 0): [0, 1]
Compute the probabilities of speculatively sampling a token: ... P[sampling A] = p(A) * (q(A) / p(A)) + p(B) * 1 * 0 = q(A) ... P[sampling B] = p(B) * 1 + p(A) * (1 - q(A) / p(A)) * 1 = q(B)
Summary: ... Exact sampling from target model (thanks to math)!

anchors.ref: Chen et al. 2023, Theorem 1 (exactness of modified rejection sampling)

anchors.quote: You basically are going to accept with probability Min 1 over this ratio of q over p. ... the larger the q is, the more likely you want to accept it. ... And otherwise you sample from this residual distribution and exit.

So this is basically rejection sampling except for rejection sampling. ... Sometimes when you reject you get nothing. ... But here we always are guaranteed to get an exact sample from the target model. ... I'm going to skip this simple proof.

provenance.filtering_note: The proof is by a two-element example only; the general statement (accept with min(1, q/p), resample from (q − p)+ normalized) is in the algorithm image at L519 and in the papers. In the example the residual [0, 1] is already normalized because max(q − p, 0) is zero on A; in general it must be divided by its sum. The term 'p(B) * 1 * 0' in L531 reads: draft proposes B (p(B)), accepted with probability min(1, q(B)/p(B)) = 1 since q(B) > p(B), and the residual puts mass 0 on A, so a rejection path to A has probability 0. Independence of acceptance decisions across positions within one pass is not discussed. Spoken evidence (1:15:04-1:15:20): the difference from plain rejection sampling is said aloud: there 'when you reject you get nothing', here a rejection still yields a token from the residual, so every pass produces an exact sample from the target. Oral filtering (1:15:20): 'I'm going to skip this simple proof': the two-token proof at L524-L532, on which this KP's statement and prompts are built, is in the code but was skipped in the talk ('basically the same arguments as rejection sampling', 1:15:28). The status stays 'said' because the proof is in the lecture text, and nothing is deferred to an assignment; a learner who only watches the video will not hear it.

prerequisites.note: p, q, accept/reject and the residual are introduced at L514-L521 before the proof.

misconceptions.belief: A draft token is accepted whenever the target also assigns it high probability, so exactness is approximate.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Acceptance is a coin with probability exactly min(1, q(x)/p(x)) and rejection redraws from max(q − p, 0) normalized; the two routes sum to q(x) (L531-L532). Nothing about 'high probability' enters.

misconceptions.belief: If the draft already samples a token with probability higher than the target does, the token is always accepted (the draft is 'confident').
misconceptions.why_wrong: That is the oversampling case p(A) > q(A), where acceptance is q(A)/p(A) < 1 (L527, L531); over-proposed tokens are exactly the ones that must sometimes be rejected to bring their rate down to q(A).

predict.q: Two-token vocabulary. Target q = [0.3, 0.7]; draft p = [0.9, 0.1]. The draft proposes A. With what probability is A rejected? Give a decimal.
predict.why: Accept with q(A)/p(A) = 0.3 / 0.9 = 1/3 (L531), so reject with 2/3. Because p oversamples A, rejections are needed to pull P[A] down to 0.3.
predict.targets_misconception: If the draft already samples a token with probability higher than the target does, the token is always accepted (the draft is 'confident').

transfer.q: Three-token vocabulary. Target q = [0.5, 0.3, 0.2]; draft p = [0.7, 0.1, 0.2]. Give the normalized residual distribution used on rejection, and verify P[sampling B] equals q(B).
transfer.why: Only A is over-proposed, so only A can be rejected, with probability 0.7 × (2/7) = 0.2; all rejected mass goes to the residual, which is entirely on B (L529-L532). C is proposed and accepted with probability 0.2 = q(C).

check.q: Three-token vocabulary [A, B, C]. Target q = [0.2, 0.5, 0.3]; draft p = [0.6, 0.2, 0.2]. On rejection the token is drawn from the normalized residual max(q − p, 0). What probability does that normalized residual assign to B? Give a decimal.
check.why: max(q − p, 0) = [0, 0.3, 0.1], which sums to 0.4 and normalizes to [0, 0.75, 0.25]. Check: rejection happens only for A, with probability 0.6 × (1 − 0.2/0.6) = 0.4, so P[B] = 0.2 + 0.4 × 0.75 = 0.5 = q(B).
check.varies: new distributions in which two tokens (B and C) are under-proposed, so the residual is split
check.invariant: the residual holds exactly the mass the draft under-proposes, which makes accept + resample equal q

retrieval.q: In the two-token proof, what is the acceptance probability for a proposed A when p(A) > q(A)?
retrieval.answer: q(A) / p(A).

retrieval.q: What distribution is sampled from when the draft token is rejected?
retrieval.answer: The residual max(q − p, 0), normalized.

retrieval.q: Write out the two routes that together give P[sampling B] = q(B).
retrieval.answer: Draft proposes B and it is accepted (p(B)·1), or draft proposes A, it is rejected (p(A)(1 − q(A)/p(A))), and the residual yields B.

steps.why: Whatever extra mass the draft puts on A it must take from B.
On rejection, mass should be added only where the draft undersamples, and here that is B alone.

steps.why: B is always accepted, since q(B)/p(B) > 1, and the residual puts 0 on A.

steps.do: Ways to end on B: propose B and accept, or propose A, reject, and draw B from the residual.
steps.why: The rejected mass p(A) − q(A) is A's excess, which equals B's deficit q(B) − p(B), so the two routes add up to q(B).

knowledge_points.label: Speculative decoding: the draft length k has a sweet spot
knowledge_points.statement: The number k of draft tokens per target pass has a sweet spot: with too few, the target's verification pass, which costs about one memory-bound decode step whether it checks one token or several, is under-used; with too many, later drafts are rejected more often (a draft token counts only if every earlier one was accepted), so the expected tokens per target pass saturates while the sequential draft work keeps growing; a draft closer to the target (higher acceptance) moves the sweet spot to larger k.

anchors.quote: And generally, if you have too few draft tokens, you're not really leveraging the batching on the target model side. ... And if you have too many, then you're going to reject more often. ... So there's a sweet spot around, in this case, three or four.
ideally, you want the model draft model to be as close to the target, which means that you want to distill it

provenance.filtering_note: Spoken only (1:15:40-1:16:04). The code gives 'e.g., 4' draft tokens (L514) and shows the paper's speed-up figure (L534) without text; why there is an optimum is only spoken: too few 'you're not really leveraging the batching on the target model side', too many 'you're going to reject more often'. 'Three or four' is read off the paper's figure and belongs to that model pair, so it is not part of the statement. The expected-tokens formula used in the prompts, E(k) = (1 - α^(k+1)) / (1 - α) for independent per-token acceptance α, is from Leviathan et al. 2022 (spec_decoding_leviathan_2022 in sources.json), not from the lecture; the compute-bound transfer extends his 'leveraging the batching' reason (author inference from decode-bandwidth-bound). The link between draft quality and k is the author's reading of 'you want the model draft model to be as close to the target' (1:16:04). Placed after speculative-sampling-exactness, where it is said.

prerequisites.note: Draft proposes k tokens, target verifies them in one pass.
Acceptance with probability min(1, q/p): where the rejections come from.

misconceptions.belief: More draft tokens per pass always means proportionally more tokens per target pass, so k should be as large as possible.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Draft token i counts only if all i - 1 before it were accepted, so its chance falls geometrically; the expected tokens per pass saturate near 1 / (1 - α), while the draft's sequential work grows linearly in k.

misconceptions.belief: The best draft length is a fixed constant (about 4) for every draft-target pair.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It depends on how often the target accepts the draft and on whether the target's verification pass is still memory-bound; 'three or four' is one paper's setting (1:15:58).

predict.q: Each draft token is accepted with probability 0.6, independently, and a draft token counts only if every earlier draft token in the pass was accepted; the target always adds one token of its own. Raising the draft length k from 4 to 16 changes the expected number of tokens per target pass how?
choices: Barely rises, from about 2.3 to about 2.5
Roughly quadruples, from about 2.3 to about 9
Roughly doubles, from about 2.3 to about 4.6
Falls, from about 2.3 to about 1.6 per pass
predict.answer: Barely rises, from about 2.3 to about 2.5
predict.why: E(k) = 1 + 0.6 + 0.6² + ... + 0.6^k = (1 - 0.6^(k+1)) / 0.4: 2.31 at k = 4 and 2.50 at k = 16, against a ceiling of 1 / 0.4 = 2.5. The draft does four times the work for 8% more tokens: 'if you have too many, then you're going to reject more often' (1:15:55).
predict.targets_misconception: More draft tokens per pass always means proportionally more tokens per target pass, so k should be as large as possible.
predict.distractor_from: 'quadruples' <- misconception: tokens per pass scale with k; 'doubles' <- applies the 0.6 acceptance once instead of compounding it; 'falls' <- expected tokens never fall with k, only the cost per useful token rises

transfer.q: A server runs the target at such a large batch that its forward pass is compute-bound rather than memory-bound. What happens to the best draft length k and to the speed-up from speculative decoding, and why?
transfer.answer: Both shrink: the best k moves toward 1 and the speed-up fades, because verifying k drafted tokens now costs roughly k times a decode step instead of about one, so rejected drafts waste real target compute.
transfer.why: The reason to draft at all is that a memory-bound target pass checks several tokens for the price of one ('leveraging the batching on the target model side', 1:15:45). When the target is compute-bound that free capacity is gone.
transfer.varies: the target's regime: compute-bound at large batch instead of memory-bound at small batch
transfer.invariant: drafting pays only while verifying extra tokens is nearly free for the target

check.q: The draft model is distilled to match the target more closely, raising its per-token acceptance rate. Which way does the best draft length k move? Start with up, down or same.
check.answer: Up: with higher acceptance, later draft tokens are still likely to survive, so the expected tokens per pass keep growing over more of k and the ceiling 1 / (1 - α) rises.
check.why: Draft token i survives with probability α^i. Raising α slows that decay, so extra draft tokens keep paying for longer; the sweet spot moves to larger k. This is why the professor wants the draft 'as close to the target' as possible (1:16:04).
check.targets_misconception: The best draft length is a fixed constant (about 4) for every draft-target pair.
check.varies: the acceptance rate instead of the target's compute regime
check.invariant: k is set by balancing tokens gained per pass against draft work and rejections

retrieval.q: In speculative decoding, what goes wrong with too few draft tokens, and what goes wrong with too many?
retrieval.answer: Too few: the target's verification pass, about as cheap for several tokens as for one, is under-used. Too many: later drafts are rejected more often, so the extra draft work buys little.

retrieval.q: Why does the expected number of tokens per target pass saturate as the draft length grows?
retrieval.answer: A draft token counts only if all earlier ones were accepted, so the i-th contributes α^i; the sum approaches 1 / (1 - α).
