The bars (expected tokens per pass) flatten under the dashed ceiling 1/(1 − α) while the cost per pass keeps rising with k, so the speed-up dots peak at a small k; a higher α moves the peak right, a compute-bound target (large B) moves it to k = 1.

knowledge_points.label: Continuous batching: iteration-level scheduling and selective batching
knowledge_points.statement: Live traffic is a ragged array (requests arrive and finish at different times, with different lengths), so Orca schedules at the level of a single decode iteration, admitting new requests every step, and batches selectively: non-attention ops run on all sequences concatenated along tokens ([3 + 9 + 5, H]) while attention runs per sequence.

anchors.quote: Batching over sequences in live traffic is tricky because: ... Requests arrive at different times (waiting for batch is bad for early requests) ... Sequences have shared prefixes (e.g., system prompts, generating multiple samples) ... Sequences have different lengths (padding is inefficient)
Training: get a dense block of tokens (batch size x sequence length) ... Inference: requests arrive and finish at different times, so you have a ragged array
Solution: iteration-level scheduling ... Decode step by step ... Add new requests to the batch as they arrive (so don't have to wait until generation completes)

Solution: selective batching ... But we might have different lengths: [3, H], [9, H], [5, H], etc. ... Attention computation: process each sequence separately ... Non-attention computation: concatenate all the sequences together to [3 + 9 + 5, H]

anchors.ref: Orca, OSDI 2022 (linked with talk at L554)

anchors.quote: The requests arrive at different times. ... They have different shared prefixes, and they have different lengths. ... It's far from this very simple training where you have these blocks of the same number of tokens all at once.

we're going to decode step by step. ... And then if you end, you just eject that sequence. ... batch is dynamically being updated with either old finished sequences being evicted and new ones coming in.

in the attention computation, you can't really do anything about this because attention depends on the length of your sequence. ... So if you have a 3 by 3, a 9 by 9 computation, you can't really share the tensor effectively.

provenance.filtering_note: The static-batching diagram (L559) is Anyscale's blog figure. The lecture does not say how new requests' prefill is interleaved with ongoing decodes (Orca runs them in the same iteration; later systems chunk prefill), nor give any throughput numbers. 'Batching only works when all sequences have the same dimensionality (right?)' (L566) is a rhetorical setup for selective batching. The reason attention cannot be concatenated is implied (each sequence attends only over its own tokens and cache) but not stated. Correction (1:19:01-1:19:34): the note above says why attention cannot be concatenated is 'implied ... but not stated'. It is stated: 'attention depends on the length of your sequence', so a 3x3 and a 9x9 score matrix cannot share one tensor, while the MLP layers, 'which takes up a lot of FLOPs', run on the concatenated 'mega sequence'. Spoken evidence (28:33-28:59): the motive given earlier is that the decode MLP's intensity equals the number of concurrent requests, which a live server does not control. How new requests' prefill is mixed into decode steps is still not said.

prerequisites.note: Continuous batching exists to keep B large during generation without making early requests wait.

misconceptions.belief: To batch requests of different lengths you must pad them to the longest, as in training.
misconceptions.why_wrong: Selective batching concatenates all sequences along the token axis for MLP and other per-token ops, so no padding is needed (L573); only attention is run per sequence (L572).

misconceptions.belief: A batch is formed when a request arrives and stays fixed until every member finishes.
misconceptions.why_wrong: That is static batching, which leaves slots idle as short sequences finish; iteration-level scheduling re-forms the batch every decode step (L561-L563).

predict.q: Three requests of 4, 7 and 12 tokens are in flight. Under selective batching, what is the shape of the tensor fed to the MLP, and how many separate attention computations run?
predict.answer: [23, H] for the MLP (4 + 7 + 12 concatenated); 3 separate attention computations, one per sequence
predict.why: Non-attention ops concatenate sequences along tokens (L573); attention processes each sequence separately (L572).
predict.targets_misconception: To batch requests of different lengths you must pad them to the longest, as in training.

transfer.q: A static-batching server forms batches of 8 and waits for all 8 to finish. Requests generate between 20 and 400 tokens. Describe what happens to GPU batch occupancy over a batch's lifetime and what iteration-level scheduling changes about it.
transfer.answer: Occupancy drops as short requests finish (down to 1 of 8 slots busy for the last, longest request), and new arrivals wait for the whole batch to drain; iteration-level scheduling refills freed slots with new requests at every decode step, keeping B near 8 and removing the wait.
transfer.why: L558 (requests finish at different times, ragged array) and L561-L563 (add new requests to the batch as they arrive).

check.q: A static-batching server runs a batch of 4 requests that generate 50, 100, 150 and 400 tokens, one token per request per decode step, admitting nothing new until all 4 finish. Averaged over the batch's 400 decode steps, what fraction of the 4 slots is busy?
check.why: Busy slot-steps = 50 + 100 + 150 + 400 = 700 out of 4 × 400 = 1,600, so 0.4375. Iteration-level scheduling would refill each freed slot at the next step and keep occupancy near 1.
check.varies: the occupancy is computed as a number instead of described
check.invariant: requests finish at different times (a ragged array); a static batch holds freed slots idle until the longest member ends
check.targets_misconception: A batch is formed when a request arrives and stays fixed until every member finishes.

retrieval.q: At what granularity does Orca schedule, and what does that let it do with new requests?
retrieval.answer: Per decode iteration; new requests join the batch as they arrive instead of waiting for generation to complete.

retrieval.q: Which computations are run per sequence and which on the concatenation under selective batching?
retrieval.answer: Attention per sequence; non-attention computation on all sequences concatenated along tokens.

retrieval.q: Name two of the three reasons the lecture gives for why batching live traffic is tricky.
retrieval.answer: Any two of: requests arrive at different times; sequences share prefixes (system prompts, multiple samples); sequences have different lengths (padding is inefficient).

prompts.self_explain: Why is attention the one operation that cannot be run on the [3 + 9 + 5, H] concatenation?

presentations.notice: listen for: attention depends on each sequence's length, so only the non-attention layers are concatenated

Under static batching a slot whose request ends early stays grey until the batch's longest request ends; iteration-level scheduling fills it at the next step, so occupancy rises and everything finishes sooner. The selective-batching panel concatenates the sequences to [Σ tokens, H] with no padding and runs attention once per sequence.

Under static batching the slots of B and C sit idle until A ends and D, E, F wait; under iteration-level scheduling each freed slot takes the next request in the following step, so the same six requests finish in 13 steps instead of 18.

knowledge_points.label: PagedAttention: block-level KV allocation, prefix sharing, copy-on-write
knowledge_points.statement: Pre-allocating a max-length KV slab per request wastes memory to internal fragmentation (unused tail) and external fragmentation (gaps between slabs); vLLM's PagedAttention stores each sequence's cache in fixed-size non-contiguous blocks mapped like OS pages, so blocks are allocated as tokens are generated and shared prefixes (system prompts, multiple samples per prompt) share physical blocks with copy-on-write.

anchors.quote: Previous status quo: ... Allocate section of KV cache for prompt and response (up to a max length) ... Problem: fragmentation (what happens to your hard drive) ... But this is wasteful since we might generate much fewer tokens (internal fragmentation)! ... Might be extra unused space between sections (external fragmentation)!
Solution: PagedAttention (remember operating systems) ... Divide the KV cache of a sequence into non-contiguous **blocks**

In general, multiple types of sharing KV caches across sequences: ... Sharing the system prompt ... Sampling multiple responses per prompt (e.g., for program synthesis) ... Solution: share prefixes, copy-on-write at the block level

Kernel to fuse block read and attention (reduce kernel launch overhead) ... Use latest kernels (FlashAttention, FlashDecoding) ... Use CUDA graphs to avoid kernel launch overhead ... Summary: use ideas from operating systems (paging) to make use of memory for dynamic workloads

anchors.ref: vLLM / PagedAttention paper (figures shown at L582-L600)

anchors.quote: you have to allocate enough buffer so that-- because you don't when you're going to stop. ... So you might have a max token limit of 1,024. ... That's internal fragmentation. ... there could be space between different requests. ... So that's just wasted space.

if you have, system prompts, then you can actually just cache these system prompts, the KV cache and the system prompts, once. ... if a lot of people are using the same system prompt, then you don't have to compute the cache for every request.

And then this is called copy on write semantics. ... if they had happened to sample let's say the same token, you just continue with that. ... But if they sample different tokens, you split the block, and then you can continue there.

Spoken evidence (1:20:19-1:20:50): both kinds of fragmentation are explained: internal, because a request's end is unknown, so a max-length buffer (1,024 tokens in his example) is reserved and mostly unused; external, gaps between requests too small to use. Requests entering and leaving every iteration is what makes a static per-request allocation fragment.

misconceptions.belief: PagedAttention makes attention itself faster.
misconceptions.why_wrong: It is a memory-management scheme: it removes fragmentation so more sequences fit and prefixes can be shared (L583-L599). The attention kernel must in fact gather from non-contiguous blocks, which vLLM fuses to avoid extra launches (L603).

misconceptions.belief: Reserving the maximum response length per request is harmless because unused memory is freed when the request ends.
misconceptions.why_wrong: While the request runs, the unused tail (internal fragmentation) and the gaps between slabs (external fragmentation) are unavailable to other requests, which caps the batch size (L584-L585).

predict.q: A server reserves a 2048-token KV slab per request. A request has a 37-token prompt and generates 60 tokens, so the slab wastes 2048 − 97 = 1951 token slots. With PagedAttention at 16-token blocks instead, how many token slots are wasted on this request?
predict.why: Paged: 7 blocks cover 97 tokens (112 slots), so 15 are wasted. The slab pays internal fragmentation for the whole unused tail (L584); paging allocates blocks as tokens arrive, so waste is under one block (L588).
predict.targets_misconception: Reserving the maximum response length per request is harmless because unused memory is freed when the request ends.

transfer.q: A program-synthesis service samples 8 completions for each 500-token prompt, 16-token blocks, Llama 2 13B cache (819,200 bytes per token). How many bytes of prompt KV cache does the request hold with and without prefix sharing, and what happens to a shared block when one sample's generation first writes into it?
transfer.answer: 419 MB with sharing (32 blocks = 512 slots × 819,200 B) vs 3.36 GB without (8 × 419 MB); on the first write the block is duplicated (copy-on-write) for the writing sample and the others keep the original.
transfer.why: Prompt blocks are shared across the 8 samples (L597, L599); 500 tokens need ceil(500 / 16) = 32 blocks; 512 × 819,200 = 419 MB (L297). Copy-on-write at the block level (L599) keeps the shared prefix intact.

check.q: With PagedAttention and 16-token blocks, a server holds 4 samples of one 300-token prompt, before any sample has generated a token. With prefix sharing, how many physical blocks hold the prompt's KV cache?
check.why: ceil(300 / 16) = 19 blocks, shared by all 4 samples (L597, L599); without sharing it would be 76. The partially filled 19th block is copied on write when a sample first appends to it.
check.varies: prompt length, sample count, and blocks are counted instead of bytes
check.invariant: the cache is stored in fixed-size blocks; samples of one prompt map to the same physical prompt blocks

retrieval.q: Name the two kinds of fragmentation the status quo suffers and what each wastes.
retrieval.answer: Internal: the unused tail of a request's max-length reservation. External: unused space between reserved sections.

retrieval.q: What is the unit of KV-cache allocation in PagedAttention, and from which field is the idea borrowed?
retrieval.answer: Non-contiguous blocks (pages), borrowed from operating systems.

retrieval.q: Give the two prefix-sharing scenarios the lecture lists and the mechanism that keeps sharing safe.
retrieval.answer: Shared system prompt; multiple samples per prompt. Copy-on-write at the block level.
